extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners who represent trademark applicants/registrants before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing competent, ethical prosecution of U.S. trademark matters before the USPTO, including signature rules, reasonable inquiry/certification obligations, supervision of non-attorneys, client and USPTO notice obligations, and related disciplinary sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applicants and registrants not domiciled within the United States must be represented by an attorney who is an active member in good standing of the bar of the highest court of any U.S. state, DC, or territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule intended to increase USPTO customer compliance, improve accuracy of trademark submissions, and safeguard integrity of the U.S. trademark register. Practitioners for foreign-domiciled clients are expected to undertake bona fide review of specimens and otherwise ensure compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a) and (c))
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory; a person electronically signing a document must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation marks that he or she has adopted as a signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a signature was entered by someone other than the named signatory or not signed by a proper person, the trademark may be subject to cancellation or the registration may be invalid. Presenting impermissibly signed filings undermines the integrity of the registration process.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP § 611.01 signature guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: TMEP § 611.01 provides that (a) the person identified as the signatory must personally sign the document (a paralegal/assistant may not sign for an attorney or other authorized signatory), (b) a person may not delegate his or her authority to sign, and (c) no person may use document-signing software to enter or electronically generate someone else's signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP is a publicly available guidance document and is cited as clear and unambiguous guidance on signature rules; practitioners are expected to follow it and cannot rely on delegation or software to create another person's signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifications under 37 C.F.R. § 11.18 (reasonable inquiry and evidentiary support)
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting any paper to the USPTO, the practitioner certifies that, to the best of the practitioner's knowledge, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, the factual contentions made in the document have evidentiary support (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting documents without reasonable inquiry or without evidentiary support can violate § 11.18(b)(1) and (b)(2), including where the filing contains false signatory information or false applicant information or specimens not demonstrating actual use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must provide competent representation to clients; examples of failing competence include accepting an unreasonably large volume of clients such that insufficient time, attention, and care are devoted; not adequately reviewing filings (e.g., specimens); not putting in place procedures to ensure compliance; and presenting documents not signed by the named signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes case management, review procedures, supervisory mechanisms, and substantive knowledge of applicable trademark requirements. Failure in these areas is a basis for discipline under § 11.101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client decision and consultation obligations (37 C.F.R. § 11.102(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must abide by the client's decisions regarding representation and consult with the client as to the means by which they are to be pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to consult or to file the classes or content the client required (example: omission of classes the client wished to include) demonstrates breach of § 11.102(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must act with reasonable diligence and promptness, which includes devoting sufficient time to client matters, maintaining procedures to ensure filings comply with USPTO rules, presenting only properly signed documents, adequately reviewing filings (e.g., specimens), and addressing issues identified by examining attorneys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays, cursory review, failing to respond to Office actions, or repeatedly filing deficient or improperly signed documents are violations of § 11.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication and consultation (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.104(a)(2) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must communicate with clients and reasonably consult about the means to accomplish the client's objectives, including counseling clients on legal requirements for trademark applications and ensuring applications are complete, correct, and signed in accordance with USPTO rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must explain differences between § 1(a) (use) and § 1(b) (intent-to-use) filings, specimen requirements, and the risks of third-party payment arrangements; failure to do so violates § 11.104.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party payment and informed consent (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who accepts compensation from someone other than the client must consult the client and obtain informed consent regarding the arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting fees from third parties without client consultation/consent (example in the Order: accepting a fee from Nestech 360 Corporation to represent another person) violates the rule and can form a basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform tribunal and present material facts (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: In an ex parte proceeding, the practitioner must inform the tribunal of all material facts known to the practitioner that will enable the tribunal to make an informed decision, whether or not the facts are adverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes conducting reasonable inquiry before filing declarations and timely informing the USPTO of improperly signed documents or other material adverse facts relied upon by examining attorneys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct involving misrepresentation includes presenting false specimens to the USPTO, signing declarations representing specimens show use in commerce without performing a reasonable inquiry, presenting documents not signed by the named signatory, and not timely informing Trademark Operations about improperly signed filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include digitally created/altered mockups, copied third‑party images, and repeated filings of specimens already identified as false by examiners; such acts violate § 11.804(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the USPTO trademark registration process—such as submitting false specimens, failing to conduct a reasonable inquiry before signing and filing, and presenting documents not signed by the named signatory—violates § 11.804(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations that undermine USPTO processes and reliance on practitioner-submitted evidence are treated as prejudicial conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision and oversight of non‑attorneys and foreign agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must supervise non‑attorneys and foreign intermediary agents, ensure they do not impermissibly enter the practitioner's signature or otherwise engage in unauthorized practice, and implement procedures (including written agreements and controls) to ensure compliance with USPTO rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: no written agreements with foreign agents, failing to monitor or prevent patterns of impermissible signature entry, and failing to put safeguards in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify clients about impermissible signatures and potential harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must notify clients when trademark documents have been impermissibly signed and explain the actual or potential significant harm to the clients' intellectual property rights arising from the impermissible signings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial or delayed notice, failure to provide written notices, or abandoning notification efforts after discovery is improper; practitioners must take reasonable steps to reach affected clients and correct records as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify USPTO Trademark Operations about impermissible signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must inform the USPTO's Trademark Operations about trademark matters containing impermissible signatures where the practitioner is counsel of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners cannot assume the USPTO already knows; failing to notify Trademark Operations about improperly signed documents is a violation when the practitioner has knowledge or should have known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to monitor USPTO correspondence, filing receipts, and accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must review USPTO filing receipts and correspondence sent to the practitioner's email, monitor USPTO accounts, and search public USPTO systems to identify filings that name the practitioner as counsel so that unauthorized or improper filings can be promptly reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order required bi-weekly searches of tmsearch and prompt written notice to Trademark Examination Policy for filings made without knowledge or consent; failure to review filing receipts (which contain signer information) is negligent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review specimens and verify actual use in commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must perform an adequate review to confirm that specimens show the mark as used in commerce before signing declarations under penalty of perjury for § 1(a) filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not file false specimens, digitally altered mockups, or copied third-party website materials as specimens. If an examining attorney identifies a specimen as false, practitioner must address the issue rather than repeatedly filing the same deficient specimen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on delegation of signing authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may not delegate his or her authority to sign trademark documents; the named signatory must personally enter the signature, and staff/assistants may not sign on behalf of the attorney or applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using document-signing software or permitting others (including foreign agents) to enter the named signatory's signature is impermissible and can invalidate filings or expose the practitioner to discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and remedial conditions for disciplinary violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary remedies may include suspension from practice before the Office (e.g., ten months), compliance with reinstatement regulations (37 C.F.R. § 11.58), probationary periods with monitoring, training requirements, disabling of USPTO accounts, prohibitions on obtaining/using USPTO accounts until reinstated, cooperation in investigations, and public publication of the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order specifies mechanics for enforcement: OED may issue Orders to Show Cause, provide 15 days to respond, request additional suspension if probation conditions are violated, require completion of USPTO Trademark Basics Boot Camp modules, bi-weekly searches and bi-monthly reporting during probation, and waiver of appeal rights in agreed settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of familiarity with USPTO resources and precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are reasonably expected to know applicable trademark prosecution rules, the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct implicated by representation of foreign-domiciled clients, and the potential disciplinary consequences, as the USPTO publishes ample guidance (TMEP, rulemaking, OED FOIA reading room, Official Gazette, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO has published numerous precedential disciplinary orders; practitioners should consult these resources and prior decisions to understand compliance expectations and consequences of violations.
